newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Ashland expects better return.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ashland expects better return.

text.p: Ashland Inc now expects its petroleum unit to be earning a return exceeding 10 percent within five years, President Paul W. Chellgren told Reuters.
The company's goal is an 11 to 13 percent after tax return on unleveraged capital for all lines of business, the chief executive noted during an interview.

With the company's cost of capital at 9 to 10 percent, he continued, 10 percent is the minimum return. Ashland Petroleum, the company's refinery and wholesale product sales arm, earned 3 percent last year, the company reported recently.
Raising Ashland Petroleum's return to 10 percent would boost its operating income to about $200 million based on the company's current investment, Chellgren said.
Noting this is about $150 million higher than the unit earned in fiscal 1996, ended September 30, he said it "would add $1.30 per share" to last year's profit of $2.97 per share.
Chellgren did not say how he expected to accomplish the increase.

Monday night he told security analysts "Ashland's board has for at least five years been regularly studying, both internally and with outside investment bankers, a wide variety of possible combinations including spearating into several companies.
"We have been unable to come up with dramatic alternatives that when fairly analyzed would clearly benefit our shareholders," Chellgren said.
He also told the analysts the company "will take action to de-emphasize our involvement in businesses which are not earning adequate returns."

The chief executive also pointed out the company believes it has made some refining and marketing accomplishments during the past few years, noting Ashland Petroleum's throughput was up last year while refining costs declined.

Chief Financial Officer J. Marvin Quinn told the analysts' meeting, which was closed to the press, that refinery runs increased 5 percent to nearly 369,000 barrels daily last year, but a $2.22 per barrel increase in Ashland's crude input costs during the year, to $20.50 per barrel, "could not be fully passed through in product prices."
Chellgren told Reuters "we like this business rationalizing" represented by the proposed Diamond Shamrock Inc/Ultramar Corp merger and the Texaco Inc/Shell Oil Co refining and marketing venture.
"I'm not aware of other imminent" proposals, he added.
